Most learners identified the 3 economic sectors but could not indicate the change in economic sector as the country becomes more developed. They thus scored 3 marks out of 7 marks. Discuss how the importance of the different economic sectors in a country change as the country becomes more developed. • Developing countries focus more on primary sector, agriculture, farming fishing and mineral extraction. • Developing countries usually exports agricultural goods or natural resources and imports value added goods from developed countries. Primary sector • Primary sector will be mechanised and modernised. • Employment in this sector will decrease. • Primary sector will change from labour intensive production methods to capital intensive production methods. Secondary sector • Employment in the secondary sectors will increase. • As developing countries develop they will become more self-sufficient in the production of value added goods. Tertiary sector • The tertiary (services) sector will grow as services needs to be rendered to the secondary and tertiary sectors, • Services such as maintenance services and banking services. 7 Up to seven marks for discussing how the importance of the different economic sectors will change as a country becomes more developed. Reference to all economic sectors required to earn full marks.

The question paper was of the same level of difficulty, as the one written in 2020. The standard of the learners’ work was lower than last year. Some of the learners could not express themselves well, due to language barriers. They thus struggled to answer some of the questions. The learners also struggled with interpreting some of the questions, which resulted in them scoring very low or even zero marks. Questions based on certain topics, e.g. stock exchange and elasticity were poorly answered. This was an indication that this part of the syllabus was either not discussed or not studied at all by the learners. Hence, it is important that teachers cover the whole syllabus to enable learners to score good marks.

Public ownership • The government owns all factors of production. Planned production • A national plan with production targets for different industries is established. • For the goods and services which are provided by the government Prices • Are not free to change in response to changes in demand and supply. Prices are fixed and controlled by the state • Shortages and physical rationing might occur Profits • Firms owned by government do not produce for profit • but what the government thinks is in the best interest of the people collectively (3 x 2) 6 A description of the features required. Fairly well answered. The majority of learners gave both positive and negative effects of a command economic system. Comment on the effectiveness of a command economic system. • Factors of production can be organised to produce public and merit goods as well as services, such as education and health care • The distribution of wealth is more equal • Goods and services provided by the government are priced so that everyone can afford them/affordability • State ownership of the factors of production allows for any “profit” made to be ploughed back into state owned enterprises • The government can make sure that factories do not cause pollution and that people work in healthy and safe conditions • High employment as government employs more workers • Government would also manage the economy to smooth out economic fluctuations • The government decides what to produce • how it will be produced • and how it will be distributed 7 Any seven

Poorly answered. Most of learners could not give the advantages of a mixed economic system, but they rather concentrated on both systems. Evaluate the merits of changing from a command economic system to a mixed economic system. • A mixed economic system will promote economic development • The public and private sector operate equally and economic resources will be utilised efficiently • Regions will be developed and improved through the planning commission of the country • Income and wealth would be more equally distributed through government welfare programmes • Consumers will be able to influence what goods and services are produced through their purchases (consumer sovereignty) • The market system will provide incentives to entrepreneurs in the form of profits and higher wages of workers • Consumers will have greater choice of producers • Competition will increase amongst rival firms, increasing quality of products and lowering prices • Foreign investment might increase 7 Up to seven marks for the advantages of a mixed economic system evaluated.

Well answered. Most learners gave a definition of trade unions and the types of trade unions. Define a trade union and give two examples of different types of trade unions. • A trade union is a workers’ organisation (1) that represents workers in their dealings with the management and owners of a firm (1) • Examples: craft union, general union, industrial union/blue collar union, white collar union (2) 4 Two marks for definition. Two marks for examples.

Fairly well answered. Learners referred to industrial action such as a strike. It is a way to resolve disputes between trade union and employer’s associations. Explain the different ways of how a dispute may be resolved if the union and employer disagree. • Trade unions negotiate with employers’ associations to bargain collectively regarding wages and working conditions • Negotiations which fail lead to conciliation. An independent person is called in to listen to both sides and tries to guide them to an agreement • If conciliations fail, arbitration is used: - an independent person acts as a judge - listens to both sides and makes a decision which is binding on both trade unions and employers’ associations • If arbitration fails, labour court is used to resolve the disagreement arising between parties (3 x 2) 6 Up to six marks for explanation of ways to reach agreement.

Ev (up to 8 marks) The advantages of inflation (Yes, because…)
• When prices are increasing, people are reluctant to spend money because they feel that goods will be cheaper in the future, thus delay purchases. May lead to a fall in demand-pull inflation.

• Decrease economic growth.

Teachers should use a variety of resources. Teachers should not just use or focus on one textbook; they should make use of other resources such as YouTube, past question papers and read the examiner’s reports. Teachers should put emphasis on the analysis of the graph, especially on the change in price and change in quantity supplied. Teachers should teach and emphasise the chain of reasoning in class discussions. Teachers should come up with debate topics to develop critical thinking and discourage learners from giving points without developments. Use real life situation, happening in the economy or in Namibia for to relate. Expose learners to the trending news on NBC and any other related economic affairs. Learners should read newspaper articles (business) to expand their vocabulary and teachers should assess learners based on the articles read. Teachers should encourage discussions in class, as well as make use of local printing media in class discussions. Teachers should teach the correct definition, by focusing on the key words of the definitions.

Teachers should emphasise the command words, such as distinguish, assess, analyse, discuss, and outline to train learners on how to answer questions. Emphasis on assessment objectives is vital. Teachers must test learners on different levels of assessment objectives. Teachers should teach learners the proper way to distinguish by using the connecting word like while in a sentence such as most public limited companies aim to make a profit, while public cooperations aim to provide essential goods and services.

Learners should only tabulate when asked to do so. Teachers should complete the syllabus on time in order to have ample time to complete revision with learners. Teachers should complete the syllabus by the end of the first term in Grade 11. Teachers are encouraged to use the prescribed textbook(s), by ensuring that the information is correct and covering the syllabus. If parts are wrong or not covered in the syllabus topics, then they should use other sources such as old textbooks. Teachers should increase the volume of written assessment work in class. Teachers must teach the syllabus and equip themselves with various credible information to enrich their subject knowledge.
